units.title: Ruth
units.subtitle: The scroll of chesed: choosing, sheltering, and a God found in human kindness

lessons.title: Ruth (1): Your people, my people
lessons.check_note: Yevamot 47b and Berakhot 7b read on Sefaria 11/11. English: JPS Tanakh gender-sensitive.

cards.title: Three widows on the road
cards.body: In Moab, **Naomi** has lost her husband and both sons. She hears that Adonai "had taken note of the people" back home, and sets out with her two Moabite daughters-in-law, **Orpah and Ruth** (1:1-6).

cards.q: What happens when Naomi tells Ruth to go back to her own people?
choices: Ruth refuses and binds herself to Naomi
cards.why: Orpah kisses her goodbye; **Ruth clings to her** and refuses to leave (1:14-17).

cards.gloss: "your people shall be my people, and your God my God" (1:16): four Hebrew words that change the history of Israel.

cards.title: When Naomi stopped arguing
cards.body: "When [Naomi] saw how determined she was to go with her, she ceased to argue with her" (1:18). **Rabbi Elazar** learns from this how to receive someone who wants to become a Jew: you may test their resolve, but once it is clear, **you stop arguing**.

cards.q: What does the Talmud learn from Naomi falling silent (1:18)?
choices: Once a person's resolve to join is clear, you stop dissuading them
Naomi didn't want Ruth to come
cards.why: Ruth becomes **the model** for choosing to join the Jewish people.
wrong_why: Naomi did test her first; the point is when to stop.
The verse says Naomi saw her determination.

cards.title: What's in the name Ruth?
cards.body: **Rabbi Yochanan**: she was called Rut because from her came **David**, who **saturated** (riva) the Holy One with songs and praises.

cards.gloss: "Call me Mara" (1:20), bitterness. Naomi says it plainly: "I went away full, and Adonai has brought me back empty." The book lets her say it.

cards.q: What name does Naomi ask to be called?
cards.why: **Mara**: "for Shaddai has made my lot very bitter" (1:20).
wrong_why: Ruth is her daughter-in-law.
Orpah went back to Moab.

cards.prompt: In the same scene, Ruth binds herself to a people and a God before anything has gone well, and Naomi names her bitterness out loud. Which voice do you recognize today?

points: "**Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.**"
Yevamot 47b: when resolve is clear, **stop arguing**.
Berakhot 7b: Ruth, ancestor of David who **saturated God with song**.
Naomi: "**Call me Mara.**"

lessons.title: Ruth (2): Under whose wings
lessons.check_note: Mishnah Berakhot 9:5 read on Sefaria 11/11. The kanaf link between 2:12 and 3:9 is in the Hebrew text itself.

cards.title: A field of strangers
cards.body: Ruth goes out to **glean** behind the reapers, and happens to come to the field of **Boaz**, a relative of Naomi's husband (2:1-3).

cards.q: The Mishnah learns from Boaz to greet people with God's name.
cards.why: **Mishnah Berakhot 9:5**, from Boaz's "Adonai be with you!" (2:4).

cards.title: A blessing for hello
cards.body: Boaz greets his workers, "Adonai be with you!" and they answer, "Adonai bless you!" The **Mishnah**: from this the Sages instituted that people **greet one another using God's name**.

cards.gloss: "under whose wings you have sought refuge" (2:12). Boaz prays that **God** will shelter Ruth, the stranger in his field.

"Spread your robe over your handmaid" (3:9). In Hebrew, "robe" here is **kanaf**, the very word for God's **wings** in 2:12. Boaz prayed for God to shelter Ruth; now Ruth asks **Boaz** to be that shelter.

cards.q: What links Boaz's blessing (2:12) to Ruth's request (3:9)?
choices: The same Hebrew word, kanaf: wings, or the corner of a robe
Both happen at the city gate
cards.why: God's **wings** and Boaz's **robe** are one word. Boaz becomes **the answer to his own prayer**.
wrong_why: Naomi isn't named in either verse.
2:12 is in the field and 3:9 at the threshing floor.

cards.gloss: "Your latest deed of loyalty is greater than the first" (3:10). The Hebrew word for loyalty is **chesed**.

cards.prompt: Boaz becomes the answer to his own prayer. Is there a prayer of yours that you could help answer?

points: Boaz's "Adonai be with you": greeting with God's name (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5).
"**Under whose wings** you have sought refuge."
"**Spread your robe**": the same word, kanaf.
Boaz becomes **the answer to his own prayer**.
**Chesed**, loyalty, greater the second time.

lessons.title: Ruth (3): The night at the threshing floor
lessons.check_note: Sanhedrin 19b read on Sefaria 11/11. Eshet chayil: Ruth 3:11 and Proverbs 31:10.

cards.title: Naomi's plan
cards.body: Naomi, who once said she came back empty, now makes a plan: "Daughter, I must seek a home for you, where you may be happy" (3:1). She sends Ruth to the threshing floor, at night, to Boaz (3:1-4).

cards.q: Boaz calls Ruth an eshet chayil, the phrase that opens the poem in Proverbs 31.
cards.why: **Eshet chayil** (3:11), the same words as Proverbs 31:10.

cards.title: Stronger than Joseph
cards.body: At midnight Boaz wakes to find a woman at his feet, and he acts with complete honor. **Rabbi Yochanan**: what Joseph is praised for, resisting temptation, was for Boaz **a small thing**, his humility. (And Palti son of Laish, he adds, was greater still.)

cards.q: How does Rabbi Yochanan compare Boaz to Joseph?
choices: What was Joseph's great strength was a small thing for Boaz
They never faced the same test
cards.why: Joseph's **power** is Boaz's **humility**: the same restraint, held more lightly.
wrong_why: He says the opposite.
He compares them precisely because they did.

cards.gloss: "what a fine woman you are" (3:11). The Hebrew is **eshet chayil**, the words that open the poem of Proverbs 31 (31:10), which many families sing at the Friday night table.

cards.q: What Hebrew phrase does Boaz use for Ruth in 3:11?
wrong_why: Go'el, redeemer, is Boaz's role.
That's the unnamed relative in chapter 4.

points: Naomi: "**I must seek a home for you.**"
Midnight at the threshing floor: Boaz acts with honor.
Sanhedrin 19b: Joseph's strength was **Boaz's humility**.
Ruth, an **eshet chayil**.

cards.title: So-and-so
cards.body: Boaz goes to the town gate, where business was done in public, and calls over the relative who has the first right to redeem: "Come over and sit down here, **So-and-so**!" (4:1). The book never gives his name.

cards.q: What is the closer redeemer's name in the Book of Ruth?
choices: He has none: he is only "So-and-so"

cards.title: The man with no name
cards.body: Why no name? In the midrash, **Rabbi Yehoshua** says Peloni Almoni really was his name. **Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman**: he was **mute from matters of Torah**. Afraid that marrying Ruth had doomed Naomi's sons, he refused her.

cards.q: What does Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman say about the unnamed redeemer?
choices: He was mute from matters of Torah, and refused Ruth out of fear
He was a stranger to Bethlehem
cards.why: **Mute in matters of Torah**: afraid of what happened to Naomi's sons, he walked away from Ruth.
wrong_why: He was a relative of Elimelech.
The midrash doesn't say that.

cards.title: The sandal
cards.body: To seal the deal, one man **takes off a sandal** and hands it to the other (4:7-8). The book stops to explain the custom, as if writing for readers who had forgotten it.

cards.he: כְּרָחֵל וּכְלֵאָה אֲשֶׁר בָּנוּ שְׁתֵּיהֶם אֶת־בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל
cards.gloss: "like Rachel and Leah, both of whom built up the House of Israel!" (4:11). The elders bless Ruth, a woman from Moab, by **the two sisters** you met in Genesis.

cards.q: Which two women do the elders name when they bless Ruth?
cards.why: "**Like Rachel and Leah**, both of whom built up the House of Israel."
wrong_why: They're matriarchs too, but not the ones named here.
Naomi and Orpah are in Ruth's own story.

points: "**So-and-so**": the redeemer without a name.
Ruth Rabbah 7:7: "mute from matters of Torah," he **refused Ruth**.
A **sandal** seals the deal.
The elders bless Ruth: **like Rachel and Leah**.

cards.title: Full again
cards.body: Boaz marries Ruth, and she bears a son. The neighbors don't say "a son is born to Ruth." They say: "**A son is born to Naomi!**" (4:13-17).

cards.q: Who do the neighbors say the baby is born to?

cards.title: Empty, then full
cards.body: In chapter 1 Naomi said, "I went away full, and Adonai has brought me back empty" (1:21). Now a child is placed in her lap, and the women name him **Obed**, father of Jesse, **father of David**. Her emptiness is filled through Ruth's loyalty.

cards.q: Why do the neighbors call Ruth's son Naomi's?
choices: Naomi, who came back empty, is made full again
cards.why: The story ends where Naomi's grief began, **reversed**.
wrong_why: The text speaks of joy, not law.
Ruth is still there; she is the one who gave Naomi this.

cards.title: Ruth saw Solomon
cards.body: The Talmud says **Ruth the Moabite lived to see the kingship of Solomon**: the stranger who chose to belong saw her great-great-grandson on the throne.

cards.q: According to Bava Batra 91b, whose reign did Ruth live to see?
wrong_why: Saul was not of her line.
Moses lived long before Ruth.

cards.prompt: The line of David begins with a woman who chose to belong. What does that say to you about who belongs?

points: "**A son is born to Naomi!**"
Naomi, **empty**, is made **full** again.
Obed, Jesse, **David**.
Bava Batra 91b: Ruth **saw Solomon's kingship**.

lessons.title: Ruth (6): Where is God in Ruth?
lessons.check_note: Count of the narrator's statements about God from the full JPS text of Ruth on Sefaria (1:6, 4:13). Ruth Rabbah 2:14 and Chullin 139b read on Sefaria 11/11. Esther 5:4 initials checked by script on the Masorah text.

cards.title: God's name, God's hand
cards.body: People in Ruth say God's name often: in blessings, in oaths, in Naomi's grief. But the **narrator** says God **did** something only **twice**: gave the people food (1:6) and let Ruth conceive (4:13). Everything else that saves anyone is **a human act**.

cards.q: How many times does the narrator of Ruth say God acted?
cards.why: **Twice**: 1:6 and 4:13. The rest is human loyalty, generosity and courage.

cards.title: Written to teach chesed
cards.body: **Rabbi Ze'eira**: this scroll contains no laws of purity or impurity, nothing forbidden or permitted. Why was it written? **To teach how great the reward is for those who do chesed**, acts of loving-kindness.

cards.q: According to Rabbi Ze'eira, why was the Book of Ruth written?
choices: To teach the reward of loving-kindness
To teach the laws of gleaning
To record the history of Moab
cards.why: No laws at all: **chesed** is the whole point.
wrong_why: He says the scroll has no laws in it.
That's not his answer.

cards.title: The hidden face
cards.body: Ruth's neighbor in the Writings goes further: the Book of **Esther never names God at all**. The Talmud asks where Esther is hinted at in the Torah, and answers with God's warning, "I will hide My face" (Deuteronomy 31:18): **haster astir** sounds like **Esther**.

cards.gloss: "let Your Majesty and Haman come today" (Esther 5:4). Read only the **first letters** of these four Hebrew words: yod, heh, vav, heh, the **four-letter Name**. God is in the story, hidden inside an ordinary sentence.

cards.q: What is hidden in the first letters of four words in Esther 5:4?
cards.why: Yod, heh, vav, heh: **God's Name**, hidden in a dinner invitation.
wrong_why: Esther's Hebrew name, Hadassah, isn't there.
Chesed isn't spelled there.

cards.title: A people growing up
cards.body: A teaching from your rabbi: the Torah can be read as a people **growing up spiritually**. First, God is a child's hero who fixes everything. Then the relationship becomes strained and complicated. In maturity, God is no longer a hand moving events, but a love that becomes **present when we make great moral choices**. Ruth is that last stage: God's shelter arrives as Boaz's robe, and God's chesed as Ruth's. The Bible scholar **Richard Elliott Friedman** traces a similar arc: God's visible presence fades across the Bible until Esther, where God is never named.

src.ref: Teaching from Jamie's rabbi (oral, as Jamie retold it); Richard Elliott Friedman, The Hidden Face of God (1995)

cards.prompt: If God is present in the moments when people choose chesed, where did you meet God this week?

points: The narrator says God acted **twice**; everything else is **human chesed**.
Ruth Rabbah 2:14: written **to teach the reward of chesed**.
Esther: God **never named**, the Name **hidden** in Esther 5:4 (Chullin 139b).
Your rabbi: a people growing up, God present **in our moral choices**.
